title-group.article-title: Mechanical and morphometric approaches to body mass estimation in rhesus macaques: a test of skeletal variables

sec.title: Objectives:
sec.p: Estimation of body mass from skeletal metrics can reveal important insights into the paleobiology of archeological or fossil remains. The standard approach constructs predictive equations from postcrania, but studies have questioned the reliability of traditional measures. Here, we examine several skeletal features to assess their accuracy in predicting body mass.

sec.title: Materials and Methods:
sec.p: Antemortem mass measurements were compared with common skeletal dimensions from the same animals postmortem, using 115 rhesus macaques (male: n=43; female: n=72). Individuals were divided into training (n=58) and test samples (n=57) to build and assess Ordinary Least Squares or multivariate regressions by residual sum of squares (RSS) and AIC weights. A leave-one-out approach was implemented to formulate the best fit multivariate models, which were compared against a univariate and a previously published catarrhine body-mass estimation model.

sec.title: Results:
sec.p: Femur circumference represented the best univariate model. The best model overall was composed of four variables (femur, tibia and fibula circumference and humerus length). By RSS and AICw, models built from rhesus macaque data (RSS=26.91, AIC=−20.66) better predicted body mass than did the catarrhine model (RSS=65.47, AIC=20.24).

sec.title: Conclusion:
sec.p: Body mass in rhesus macaques is best predicted by a 4-variable equation composed of humerus length and hind limb midshaft circumferences. Comparison of models built from the macaque versus the catarrhine data highlight the importance of taxonomic specificity in predicting body mass. This paper provides a valuable dataset of combined somatic and skeletal data in a primate, which can be used to build body mass equations for fragmentary fossil evidence.

sec.title: Introduction
sec.p: The estimation of body mass from skeletal remains is a widespread practice across organismal biology, and especially within anthropology – from archeology (Pomeroy and Stock, 2012; Auerbach and Ruff, 2004; Elliott et al. 2015a) and paleoanthropology (Grabowski et al. 2015; Will et al., 2015; Jungers et al. 2016) to the forensic sciences (Schaffer, 2016; Jeanson et al. 2017). However, the popularity of body size estimation is complicated by the search for appropriate skeletal predictors, the most appropriate reference samples, and the most accurate equations (Ruff, 2003; Elliott et al. 2015a, 2015b; Grabowski et al., 2015; Burgess et al., 2018; Conroy, 1987). For example, the majority of reference data are collected from recent human populations with the goal of estimating body size specifically within the human lineage (e.g. Grabowski et al. 2015, Rainwater, 2022), and body mass estimates for non-human primates have been shown to exhibit a high degree of error possibly because many correlate skeletal and body mass data from different individuals (Smith 1985; Delson et al., 2000; Perry et al. 2018). In this study, we use the CPRC-NYU Skeletal Collection, a unique sample of rhesus macaques (Macaca mulatta) with paired postmortem skeletal and antemortem somatic data, to explore the accuracy of common skeletal measurements as predictors of catarrhine body mass.

An animal’s body size is a highly informative feature, from which important insights into ecology may be gained (Elliott et al. 2015b; Ruff, 2002; Plavcan 2012; Smith 1996). Body size is a particularly crucial metric in the paleosciences as a relatively straightforward way to access the living somatic context of animals for which little to no soft tissues remain. Cercopithecids are a particularly interesting family because of the diversity of habitat usage in extant members, ranging from open plain papionins like Theropithecus and Papio to arboreal specialists like Miopithecus (Barton et al., 1992; Elton 2002; Cords 2012; Abie et al., 2017). In many cases, body size can be directly correlated to patterns of habitat use (Granatosky, 2018). Understanding the relationship between skeletal dimensions and body mass in rhesus macaques not only benefits our understanding of macaque size evolution, but potentially ecological niche utilization for primates more broadly.

The previous literature on mechanical body mass reconstruction in primates relies heavily on a few measures of key load-bearing joints, especially the superior-inferior (SI) breadth of the femoral head (Ruff 1991; Rafferty et al. 1994; McHenry 1992; Grine et al. 1995; Elliott et al. 2015a, 2015b). However, joint surfaces are complex structures with important functional relationships with features other than mass, including joint excursion (Ruff 1988; MacLatchy and Bossert, 1996; Hammond et al. 2016). Studies have shown that measures of midshaft cross-sectional geometry predict body mass better than SI femoral head breadth does (Ruff, 2003; Elliott et al. 2015a; see also Jungers et al., 1998; Delson et al., 2000).

Because most catarrhines are quadrupedal, the distribution of gravitational loading across the body is likely not the same as that observed in bipedal human populations. Primates are commonly characterized as ‘hind limb-driven’, exhibiting greater ground reaction forces in the hind limb compared with the fore limb during locomotion, in contrast with largely fore limb-driven non-primate mammals (Kimura et al. 1979; Demes et al. 1994). However, the distribution of ground reaction forces is variable in primates – notably, catarrhines exhibit approximately equal fore limb to hind limb vertical peak forces during terrestrial locomotion (Kimura et al. 1979; Kimura 1985, 1992; Reynolds 1985; Demes et al. 1994; Schmitt and Hanna, 2004). This pattern may be the result of the evolution of vertical climbing in the primate lineage (Hanna et al. 2017; Dickinson et al. 2021). Hirasaki et al. (1993) showed similar levels of fore and hind limb propulsion in the terrestrial Japanese macaque, whereas the more arboreal long-tailed macaque exhibited greater propulsion through the hind limb (Hanna and Schmitt 2011). As a closely related and primarily terrestrial species, rhesus macaques also exhibit a more equal distribution of limb forces similar to that observed in the Japanese macaque (Kimura 1992). As a result, the importance of hind limb joint measures like femoral head SI breadth may be comparatively reduced.

In the context of fragmentary fossil evidence, it is most convenient to be able to use a single commonly recovered element, such as a robust component like the femoral head, to reconstruct important somatic measures like body mass. However, the use of additional body shape dimensions like bi-iliac breadth and stature are argued to considerably improve the accuracy of body mass predictions (Auerbach and Ruff 2004). This morphometric approach canonically treats the body as a cylinder where bi-iliac breadth is the diameter of the cylinder, stature is its height, and the cylinder’s volume is equivalent to body mass (Ruff 1991, 1994, 2000, 2006; Ruff et al. 1997, 2005; Auerbach and Ruff, 2004; Pomeroy and Stock, 2012; Walker et al. 2018). The addition of these body shape measures aims to increase the accuracy of mass predictions by accounting for differences in load distribution through the pelvis, which are left out in mechanical approaches (Walker et al. 2018). This approach, however, requires the general body shape of the reference sample to approximate that of the test specimen, which may not be knowable in extinct animals.

Additionally, in humans, body shape is also thought to be interrelated with the geometric dimensions of hind limb midshaft cross-sections (Ruff 1995). This signal appears to be stronger in the femur compared to the tibia, the structure of which is more responsive to individual lifetime activity patterns (Stock 2006; Ruff 1994; Ruff 1995). However, recent analysis of the correlation between femur and tibia midshaft geometry with bi-iliac breadth have revealed only weak relationships. Because of studies showing that midshaft geometry predicted body mass most accurately out of an array of skeletal variables (see Elliott et al. 2015b; see also Jungers et al., 1998; Delson et al., 2000; Ruff et al. 2003), the relationship between bone midshafts and body shape could make the addition of proportion measurements unnecessary. The extent to which body shape metrics improve mechanical mass estimation, as well as the confounding impact of adding these measures into equations based on possibly highly correlated skeletal variables, needs to be investigated further.

Here, we use a unique population of rhesus macaques with matched somatic and skeletal data to compare body mass with a suite of common skeletal metrics including limb length, joint breadth, and limb circumference. In doing so, we aim to establish which features, or combination of features, most accurately predict living mass. We also combine these comparisons with a measure of bi-iliac breadth to assess whether including a measure of body shape improves mass estimation accuracy.

sec.title: Sample
sec.p: We collected paired somatic and skeletal measurements from individuals within a cross-sectional sample of free-ranging rhesus macaques from Cayo Santiago, Puerto Rico, managed by the Caribbean Primate Research Center (CPRC) of the University of Puerto Rico. These measures were used to construct both single and multi-variable Ordinary Least Squares (OLS) regressions to assess the accuracy of individual skeletal variables (and combinations thereof) in predicting body mass in Macaca mulatta.

As part of the CPRC population management program, two rhesus macaque social groups were removed from Cayo Santiago in 2016 (Group HH) and 2018 (Group KK). A large somatometric protocol was undertaken on each animal as part of the protocols of the Cayo Biobank Research Unit. The somatometric protocol was approved by the Institutional Animal Care and Use Committee of New York University and of the University of Puerto Rico Medical Sciences Campus. After euthanasia, the cadavers were macerated using a warm-water method and the skeletons are now housed at the CPRC-NYU Cayo Santiago Skeletal Collection at New York University.

Somatic measurements were collected on the specimens prior to euthanasia. Skeletal measurements were collected postmortem after maceration of these tissues. The social groups were of similarly low rank on the island at the time of removal. As a result, these groups are physically comparable to each other, but they may also exhibit differences relative to individuals from higher-ranked groups. Individuals were weighed with a digital balance to an accuracy of 0.1 g. Body mass collection protocol for this sample is also described in Turcotte et al. (2022). The cross-sectional sample includes all ages, except 2-year-olds, who were removed for assessment for entry into the CPRC’s Specific Pathogen Free (SPF) colony, as per CPRC’s protocol. A total of n=115 specimens were included in this analysis, and those with pathologies were omitted. Individuals were classified into two groups: >2 with epiphyses present (EP; n=94) or <2 with epiphyses absent (EA; n=21). Measures requiring epiphyseal dimension (i.e., joint breadth) were performed only on the >2 aged specimens.

sec.title: Measurement Protocols
sec.p: Individuals were randomly sorted by computer generator into a sex-balanced training group (n=58) and a test group (n=57). The training group was used to assess skeletal predictors of body mass and the influence of somatic body frame size (e.g., bi-iliac breadth) on body mass estimation equations (see section 2.2.1). The test group was used for the evaluation of model fit between the uni- and multivariate models constructed in this paper as well as the univariate model developed by Perry et al. (2018) (see section 2.2.2).

Somatic measurements were collected for bi-iliac breadth, and were measured with sliding calipers between the widest points across the iliac crests (see Fig. 1). Skeletal measurements were collected for: 1) limb lengths; 2) joint breadths; and 3) limb midshaft circumferences, and were collected upon dry bone material. Skeletal long bone lengths were measured using a standard osteometric board. When epiphyses were unfused but present, the elements were refitted with museum curation putty and measured together. Putty added a very negligible distance to the measurement of long bone length. Joint breadths were measured with calipers, and midshaft circumference measurements were quantified with tape. All body mass, skeletal and somatic measurements were log-transformed before analysis.

sec.title: Skeletal Predictors of Body Mass
sec.p: Joint breadths from the fore- and hind limbs [i.e., epicondyle breadth of the humerus, SI femoral head breadth, tibial plateau breadth] are compared with midshaft circumference, which are believed to better reflect the living mass of an individual (Squyres and Ruff, 2015; Perry et al. 2018; Ruff et al. 2018). Long bone lengths are also included in our comparison, as these elements bear a similar relationship to body mass as does overall stature (Duyar and Pelin, 2003; Rastogi, 2009).

The relative predictability of each univariate skeletal feature is assessed using coefficients of determination derived from Ordinary Least Squares (OLS) regressions. The use of regression statistics to estimate body mass from skeletal material is standard in anthropology, with applications for archaeological humans (Kurki et al. 2010; Pomeroy and Stock, 2012; Ruff et al. 2012), hominoid fossil specimens (McHenry, 1992; Ruff et al. 1994, 2006; Trinkaus and Jelinek 1997; Ruff 2010; Grabowski et al., 2015), as well as platyrrhines and catarrhines generally (Perry et al. 2018). Statistical analyses in this study were conducted in R (R Core Team, 2021) via the package lazyeval (Wickham 2002).

For the purposes of understanding variation within single skeletal metrics, OLS regressions were performed first on the complete training dataset, and then on subgroups by 1) presence/absence of epiphyses and 2) by sex in the skeletally mature individuals. Analysis of Variance (ANOVA) tests were used to ascertain whether there were significant differences within each subgroup (i.e., epiphyses present v. absent and male v. female). However, for the purposes of broad applicability to body mass reconstruction in catarrhine fossil remains, the analysis of body mass estimation focuses primarily on Epiphyses Present sample in which sex is grouped.

Toward the construction of equations predicting body mass from skeletal metrics, data were analyzed in a hierarchy. First, we examined the grouped data, which included specimens both with and without epiphyses. Second, just the specimens for which epiphyses were present or could be refitted (called Epiphyses Present) were considered. We obtained the best fit univariate and multivariate model associated with each grouping. As a result, a total of four models were constructed from the training data, in the following manner.

Residual sums of squares (RSS) were extracted from the OLS regression models, which measure the amount of variance within a dataset not explained by the regression model itself. RSS values were used as measures of model fit, where a lower RSS represented the superior model fit. The best univariate model was selected based on RSS value.

Multivariate models were constructed by iteratively adding each possible second variable to each univariate model (see protocol in Rubin et al. 2018). ANOVAs were used to determine if the RSS values from the 2-variate model were significantly different from the univariate model. The best fit 2-variate model was subsequently selected for comparison with 3-variate models. The process was completed when the addition of variables did not result in a significant improvement in model RSS performance. This protocol was performed using all specimens for each variable’s length and circumference, and was repeated on specimens with epiphyses to include joint breadth measures.

Morphometric approaches to the estimation of body mass employ multivariate regressions including the above skeletal variables alongside measures of body dimension. In this study, we utilized antemortem bi-iliac breadth as a proxy estimate of body frame.

sec.title: Evaluation of Model Fit
sec.p: The four models described above were constructed using the training dataset. These models were subsequently evaluated on the test dataset in order to quantify model performance using a novel dataset. In addition, we ran the catarrhine body mass estimate equation established in Perry et al. (2018) to compare the models constructed in this study with a method previously established in the literature for a total of 5 model evaluations. The Perry et al. (2018) equation is a well-fit Reduced Major Axis (RMA) regression (R2=0.92, % standard error of estimate = 7.5) built from 7 catarrhine species (total individuals n=95), including 3 papionins.

Substitution of the test data produced a predicted body mass value for each of the 5 models detailed above. These predicted values were compared against actual body mass values for these specimens within a reduced major axis (RMA) regression model. Model fitness was assessed on the basis of reduced sum of squares (RSS) and Akaikes information criterion (AIC) weights.

sec.title: Skeletal Predictors of Body Mass
sec.p: The OLS regression statistics are presented in Table 1 for each univariate length and circumference variable for the grouped (Epiphyses Absent and Epiphyses Present) data. Table 2 contains the grouped data and sex-specific data for joint breadth, which only used Epiphyses Present specimens. RSS scores indicate that humerus length exhibited the best fit with body mass (RSS=0.89) (Table 1). Generally, long bone length measures exhibited a lower range of RSS values, and therefore a better fit, than either bone circumference or joint breadth.

ANOVA comparisons of the EA and EP length and circumference data demonstrated no significant differences in the level of variability in the univariate data (Table 3). Additionally, there were no differences between sexes within the EA data (Table 3). However, sex differences were observed in a subset of the EP data variables including humerus length (p=0.002), femur length (p=0.036), fibula length (p=0.042) (see Table 3), femur midshaft circumference (p=0.008) and tibia midshaft circumference (p=0.039) (see Table 4). There were no sex differences observed in joint breadth (Table 2).

sec.title: Grouped Data
sec.p: The addition of a second variable to the univariate models significantly improved model prediction. The best-fit bivariate model included humerus length and humerus circumference (RSS=0.6, p<0.001). The addition of a third variable produced only one significant model improvement with fibula circumference (RSS=0.54), p=0.021) (Table 5). The addition of the frame size proxy measurement bi-iliac breadth significantly improved upon the univariate model but not any of the bivariate models (see Tables 5 and 6).

sec.title: Epiphyses Present Data
sec.p: Within the Epiphyses Present dataset, the best univariate model used femur circumference (RSS=1.08) (Tables 3, 6). The addition of a second variable yielded several significantly better fit models, the best of which added humerus length to femur circumference (RSS=0.73, p<0.001) (Table 6). Several joint breadth variables yielded lower RSS scores but further comparison of AIC weights demonstrated that these were not better fit models (e.g., femur bicondylar breadth: AIC=−201.69) compared with the univariate model (AIC=−226.85) (Table 7). This discrepancy is likely due to differences in sample size between EA and EP sample sets (see Table 3). Addition of a third variable improved the model fit by including tibia circumference alongside femur circumference and humerus length (RSS=0.61, p=0.002) (Table 6). The addition of a fourth variable yielded one significant improvement to model fit (fibula circumference alongside tibia circumference, femur circumference, and humerus length; RSS = 0.53, p = 0.006). Adding a fifth variable did not significantly improve model fit (Table 6). The optimal model built from the EP data was a four-variable model including femur circumference, humerus length, tibia circumference and fibula circumference.

sec.title: Model Comparison
sec.p: Comparison of the five models (Table 8) demonstrated that the 4-variable model based on the EP data had the lowest RSS score (RSS=26.912) and the best fit AIC score (−20.659). The single variable model (RSS=32.688; AIC=−11.72) and the 3-variable model (RSS=28.81; AIC=−17.52) scored similarly. The model built from Perry et al.’s (2018) pan-catarrhine data achieved the highest RSS score (RSS=65.47) and AIC score (AIC=20.239), indicating a relatively worse fit.

sec.title: Discussion
sec.p: In this study, we evaluated skeletal dimensions in rhesus macaques from Cayo Santiago to determine the best performing variables to estimate body mass. This skeletal dataset is an invaluable resource for investigating important taxonomic questions by elucidating the boundaries of intraspecific variation, especially in the context of a wide-ranging and ecologically diverse genus such as Macaca (see Kenyon-Flatt and von Cramon-Taubadel, 2023). Additionally, understanding body size variation is critical to paleoanthropology as it represents a key component of how an animal interacts with its habitat. Body size and size dimorphism are also associated with myriad elements of living social behavior including habitat use (Smith and Jungers, 1997; Granatosky et al., 2018), degree of male-male competition (Clutton-Brock and Harvey, 1997; Gordon, 2006; Plavcan and van Schaik, 1992; Plavcan and van Schaik, 1997; Lindenfors, 2002), and mating system (Plavcan, 2001).

Our analysis shows that the most accurate predictions of body size were based on a multivariate model built from femur circumference, humerus length, tibia circumference and fibula circumference (Table 8). The best univariate model was constructed from femur circumference in the EP dataset.

Importantly, this paper provides both methods for estimating body mass from the best fit variables and an important resource for paleoprimatology. One of the primary methodological issues concerning fossil analyses has to do with the incomplete and fragmentary nature of the remains (Grabowski et al., 2015; Ruff and Niskanen, 2018). The majority of fossil primates, for example, are represented only by isolated elements (Brassey et al. 2018). This flexible dataset enables researchers to create predictive models from any combination of common measurements applied to skeletal remains. The ability to reconstruct body mass from fractional material is a particularly powerful tool for researchers studying extinct specimens.

In this comparison of the skeletal predictors of body mass, length and circumference measurements exhibited a similar range for RSS scores between 0.89–2.89. Joint breadth RSS scores were generally higher, indicating greater unexplained variation, between 1.52–3.07 (Table 2). The addition of a frame size measurement (i.e., bi-iliac breadth) did generally improve model fitness, but did not represent a component of the optimal models. The best fit univariate model differed depending on whether the EA dataset was included. Circumference measures formed part of the best fit model only in the EP group, indicating the role of mechanical activity in the shaping of long bone geometry during ontogeny. Because rhesus macaque infants engage substantively in clinging (Turnquist and Wells 1994), these individuals may not spend enough time in terrestrial quadrupedalism to load the bone shaft sufficiently to reflect body mass (see Willie et al. 2020).

Although femoral head diameter is one of the most commonly used metrics for predicting body mass it was among the poorest variables identified in this study for that purpose by RSS score (RSS=3.07). Indeed, the joint breadth measurements performed poorly as a group (see Tables 2, 7). This may be a product of sample size in this study, but it may also be an outcome of the multiple functions of joints as both load-bearing structures and facilitators of mobility. There is a physical constraint to the accumulation of bone in the articular zones of free joints, especially ball-and-socket joints like the femoral head, before movement is impaired. Alternatively, femoral head diameter may be more strongly reflective of body mass in bipeds (wherein each hind limb experiences supports an individual’s full body weight during the single limb support phase of walking) than in quadrupeds, wherein body weight is distributed across both fore limbs and hind limbs during gait. Femoral head breadth is the most frequently used metric for reconstructing body mass in hominids (Ruff et al., 2018), but it appears that there are viable, and in some instances superior, alternatives. Other elements of morphology, specifically limb length and circumference, exhibit a better fit relationship with body mass, at least in the present study.

For the EP group, long bone midshaft circumference appears to be the most effective tool for predicting body mass, both in the univariate and multivariate models. There is a complex relationship between long bone geometry and loading history, modulated by genetics and the material properties of bone (Willie et al. 2020). Bone is a living tissue that responds dynamically to loads placed upon it through the coordinated action of bone-depositing osteoblasts and tissue-removing osteoclasts. Bone is formed or remodeled when the tissue experiences loads deviating either above or below its regulatory mechanostat, the level of optimal strain (see Frost 1987). Bone is lost during chronic underuse and is gained in response to habitual loading. Following these principles of bone adaptation, geometric properties are a well-known reflection of a bone’s loading history (see Ruff and Hayes, 1992; Larson, 2015; Willie et al. 2020), where tissue accumulation deviating from a bone’s centroid indicates the buttressing of these tissue regions against mechanical failure.

Circumference was used here in order to make these data accessible for researchers without access to 3D imaging technologies. Though it is a coarse measure compared to cross-sectional geometric properties, we found external midshaft dimensions sufficient for the accurate estimation of body mass. Circumference is most directly related to the geometric property cross-sectional area or the amount of tissue in a given cross-section. Cross-sectional area is a proxy for bone strength in compression, which logically would vary according to body mass. Further investigations into this material should expand to include internal geometric properties.

Though rhesus macaques are not as hind limb-driven as most primates in terms of ground reaction forces, from chimpanzees to spider monkeys (Demes et al. 1994; Hanna et al. 2005), the optimal model includes mostly hind limb measures. Evidence from musteloids shows that body mass is highly correlated with fore limb geometric properties in more fore limb-driven species (Fabre et al. 2013). The prevalence of hind limb features in the rhesus macaque models may be the result of the complex loading environment of the hind limb bones, particularly the femur, during both positional behavior and locomotion. The bent-knee posture of the hind limb loads the bones beyond simple compression, and applied forces may not align with the maximum principal axis of the bone (Demes 2001; Willie et al. 2020). Loading in these atypical planes may be more likely to produce bone deposition, and therefore may be more informative about variation in characteristics like body size (Willie et al. 2020).

Further, ranking via RSS and AIC scores demonstrates species specificity of these models. That is, models built from macaque data better predict macaque body mass than equations based on a catarrhine dataset. This intuitive finding is an important step to more accurately reconstruct the living world of extinct primates. An effort must be made to match fossil specimens with the most relevant living population. Evidence suggests that skeletal morphology may vary significantly between even closely-related species of macaques. Elements of craniodental and pelvic shape have proven effective at discriminating macaque species (Grunstra et al. 2017; Kenyon-Flatt et al., 2020), highlighting the necessity of family-level specificity in body mass reconstruction models. Efforts like the current study to improve the availability and integration of primate datasets are critical both for understanding intraspecific variation and as reference samples for past populations.

One complicating factor in estimating body mass across taxa is the issue of body composition. Body mass is an amalgam used to describe a combination of skeletal material and all soft tissue volume, including but not limited to lean muscle, fat and skin. These different tissues do not share the same mechanical relationship with underlying bone nor the same developmental processes. Studies analyzing the relationship between skeletal metrics and individual soft tissue metrics have demonstrated stronger predictive ability of bone cross-sectional and joint surface properties for lean mass rather than overall body mass (Ruff et al. 1991; Semanick et al. 2005; Pomeroy et al. 2017). Because the rhesus macaques observed in this study come from a food-provisioned colony, it is possible that the fat composition of these animals exceeds the distribution found in wild populations. Differing levels of fat to skeletal muscle, for instance, may exhibit distinct signatures on long bone morphology independent of global changes.

Additionally, macaques, like many other primate species, experience seasonal changes in their body masses. These changes are attributed to factors such as food availability, particularly in wild primate populations which do not benefit from nutritional supplementation (Plavcan et al., 2005; Glander et al., 2006; Hanya and Chapman, 2013). For example, wild chimpanzees exhibited significantly greater body masses during the wet season, characterized by increased food availability, than during the dry season. However, these animals were heaviest during periods of external provisioning (Pusey et al., 2005). This pattern is common to primates in regions where seasonality dictates food availability (Wright, 1999; Huck et al., 2011; Gordon et al., 2013; Gordon et al., 2016; Irwin et al., 2015). Another factor contributing to seasonal body mass variation is reproduction. The rhesus macaques observed in this study were provisioned, but females accumulate fat mass during periods of mating whereas male fat reserves are depleted during the same time period (Higham et al., 2011; Lee 2019; Bercovitch et al., 2003). The rhesus macaques in this study were sampled outside of mating season but the fundamental issue persists, in which skeletal-based body mass estimates necessarily average away any seasonal variation within an individual.

sec.title: Conclusions
sec.p: Body mass in rhesus macaques is best predicted by a 4-variable equation composed of long bone circumference measures and humerus length. However because of the high covariation in terms, the univariate model based on femur circumference performs to a similar RSS score. Both the univariate and multivariate models built from rhesus macaque data perform better than the model combining catarrhine species, highlighting the importance of species specificity in body mass prediction. This is an invaluable dataset for researchers interested in macaques, and particularly for those investigating the paleobiology of extinct macaques. We also hope that our analysis and the availability of our data will help researchers to build comprehensive body mass estimates from fragmentary evidence, a powerful tool for fossil studies.

caption.p: Skeletal measurements performed on long bones, from left to right: humerus, ulna, radius, femur, tibia and fibula. Each bone was measured for length (L) and circumference (C). Joint breadths were measured on the humerus (JB.heb: humerus epicondylar breadth), the femur (JB.fh: femoral head superior-inferior breadth; JB.fbb: femur bicondylar breadth), and the tibia (JB.tp: tibial plateau breadth).

Ordinary Least Squares (OLS) Regression statistics for each univariate variable compared with body mass. Terms m and y refer to slope and y-intercept of the regression line, respectively. Adjusted R2 (adjR2) measures the goodness of fit of the regression. Residual sum of squares (RSS) measures data variance not explained by the model.

Ordinary Least Squares (OLS) Regression statistics for each univariate joint breadth separated by sex. Intergroup differences are assessed by ANOVA. Terms m and y refer to slope and y-intercept of the regression line, respectively. Adjusted R2 (adjR2) measures the goodness of fit of the regression. Residual sum of squares (RSS) measures data variance not explained by the model.

OLS regression statistics for each univariate long bone length separated by age group Epiphyses Absent (EA) and Epiphyses Present (EP), and then within each age group by sex. Intergroup differences are assessed by ANOVA. Signifcant results are bolded.

OLS regression statistics for each univariate long bone circumference separated by age group Epiphyses Absent (EA) and Epiphyses Present (EP), and then within each age group by sex. Intergroup differences are assessed by ANOVA. Significant results are bolded.

Model fit assessments in the grouped (EA+EP) data assessing length (L), circumference (CF) and the morphometric biiliac breadth variable. The univariate model is compared with new models with iteratively added terms, by residual sum of squares (RSS) and evaluated with ANOVA. Significant results are bolded.

Model fit assessments in the Epiphyses Present (EP) data, assessing length (L), circumference (CF) and the morphometric biiliac breadth variables. The univariate model is compared with new models with iteratively added terms, by residual sum of squares (RSS) and evaluated with ANOVA. Significant results are bolded.

Model fit assessments in the Epiphyses Present (EP) data. The univariate model is compared with new models with iteratively added joint breadth terms. Model fit is assessed by AIC weight. Original model AIC weights are listed at the top of the table.

Comparisons of residual sum of squares (RSS) and Akaikes Information Criterion (AIC) weights between the two univariate (SV) models and multivariate models (MV) for both grouped ages (g) and Epiphyses Present-data only (ep). A Catarrhine model (from Perry et al. 2018) is provided for contrast.
